claims.claim: Sync workers each hold one request for the whole insurer call, so by Little's law 40 req/s at about 400 ms keeps about 16 of 17 workers busy (about 95% utilisation), and a slowdown to 1.5 s would need about 60 workers
claims.measured: python-flask I/O-wait test (10 ms wait, 256 connections): 276 req/s, p50 915 ms, CPU 18%
claims.why: The I/O test shows that sync Flask stalls on waits, but it used a 10 ms wait and an unknown worker count, so it cannot check worker counts or utilisation at 200–600 ms insurer latency, which is plain arithmetic on the team's figures.

claims.claim: Switching to gthread workers raises concurrency with the existing stack and is the first thing to try
claims.measured: I/O wait: gthread 374 req/s (p50 678 ms) vs sync 276 req/s (p50 915 ms), about 1.35x
claims.why: Throughput did go up under I/O wait, so the direction is right, but the measured gain is small (about 1.35x) and far below gevent's.

claims.claim: gevent workers are well suited to this I/O-wait pattern
claims.measured: I/O wait: gevent 2,956 req/s (p50 71 ms) vs sync 276 req/s and gthread 374 req/s
claims.why: gevent gave about 10.7x the sync Flask throughput and about 8x gthread's on the I/O-wait test.

claims.claim: Async Flask / ASGI is a large migration that doesn't pay off for this problem
claims.measured: I/O wait: python-fastapi 5,901 req/s vs flask-gevent 2,956 and sync flask 276
claims.why: Measured ASGI throughput under I/O wait is the best Python result (about 2x gevent, 21x sync), but 'doesn't pay off' weighs migration cost against need at 40 req/s, and the measurements don't cover migration cost.
